name: Opportunity Green (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: almost all of the result is the IMO Fund's just-transition money for climate-vulnerable countries, which are not yet named (small island and least developed states first), and the rest is tonnes that spare people everywhere; spread by world population for want of a country split.
summary: Opportunity Green (London and Brussels) uses law, policy and analysis to cut shipping and aviation emissions: it supports climate-vulnerable countries at the International Maritime Organization, runs the SASHA Coalition of clean-fuel companies and brings legal cases; this model counts its part in the two policies its work of June 2022 to March 2026 pressed most, both still pending (it spent £2.54M in the year to March 2026): the IMO's Net-Zero Framework for shipping, whose adoption was adjourned and is due for decision in December 2026, and the EU's proposal to extend emissions trading to more international flights. At the defaults the result is negative, −0.11 years of healthy life per $1,000: on the site's values the framework's tonnes are worth far less than ships' extra fuel costs (about $300 a tonne by the IMO's own impact assessment, about half of it borne in poorer importing countries), and the part of the IMO Fund's revenue that would go to climate-vulnerable countries as development aid makes up only part of the difference; even the sign is uncertain. The sign turns on how much of the Fund reaches those countries and what that aid does, the compliance cost per tonne and who bears it; Opportunity Green's share of the advocacy is small (about 3%), and both branches are discounted for missing data.

IMO Net-Zero Framework: tonnes of CO₂e a year it would cut, first five years in force

source.title: Transport & Environment (April 2025), IMO Net-Zero Framework: assessing the impact of the IMO's draft Net-Zero Framework
source.page: pp. 2, 4-6: chart 'The new measure will fail to deliver IMO's own emission targets' (business as usual against the 2025 deal) and the yearly bars of p. 6
source.quote: The IMO Net-Zero Framework sets total GHG emissions from shipping to decrease to only 842.4 Mt CO2e by 2030 and to 530 Mt CO2e by 2035

rows.explainer: Shipping's well-to-wake emissions under the framework against business as usual, read from T&E's charts (built on the IMO's own comprehensive impact assessment by DNV): business as usual about 950 Mt a year in 2028 rising to 980 Mt by 2033; under the framework about 855 Mt in 2028, 842 Mt in 2030 and 750 Mt in 2033. The gap over the first five compliance years averages about 130 Mt a year (95 Mt in the first year to about 230 Mt in the fifth). Range: 70 Mt (a later start and weaker post-2030 prices) to 200 Mt (T&E's text, which puts 2035 at 530 Mt, below its own bars). Whether the deal is adopted, and how much of it is delivered, are rows below.

rows.label: IMO Net-Zero Framework: yearly revenue of the IMO Net-Zero Fund

source.title: Transport & Environment (April 2025), IMO Net-Zero Framework: assessing the impact of the IMO's draft Net-Zero Framework
source.quote: While the framework should be in a position to generate approx. revenues of $10 billion per year until 2035

rows.explainer: Payments for remedial units by ships that miss the targets go to the IMO Net-Zero Fund: about $10 billion a year until 2035 (T&E, from the IMO's impact assessment). Range $6-14 billion: more ships may buy surplus units from others, or pay rather than switch fuels. These payments are transfers from shipping to the Fund, so they are not a compliance cost (docs/normalization.md 2.21).

rows.label: IMO Net-Zero Framework: share of the Fund's revenue going to climate-vulnerable countries' just transition, first five years

source.title: Transport & Environment (April 2025), IMO Net-Zero Framework: assessing the impact of the IMO's draft Net-Zero Framework
source.quote: revenues available for a just and equitable transition would also dry up rapidly dropping from an estimated $6.65 billion available by 2028 to a mere $2.52 billion by 2031, with no available funds thereafter

rows.explainer: How the Fund will be spent is not yet decided: rewards for zero- and near-zero-emission fuels, and a just and equitable transition for developing countries (adaptation, capacity, loss and damage), the part Opportunity Green presses for. T&E's case where fuel rewards come first gives the just transition about $6.65 billion of roughly $9.6 billion in 2028, falling to $2.5 billion by 2031 and nothing from 2032: about two fifths over five years. Our judgment, 40% (10% if fuel rewards take nearly all, 70% if the just transition is put first).

rows.label: EU emissions trading extended to flights leaving Europe for destinations within 5,000 km: CO₂ a year newly covered

source.title: GreenAir News (21 July 2026), Commission proposes a limited extension of the ETS to international departing flights from Europe
source.quote: It assessed around 21 million tonnes of CO2 would be covered under the 5,000km radius proposal
source.note: The assessment quoted is Transport & Environment's; other coverage of the proposal gives about 19 Mt.

rows.explainer: The Commission's proposal of 17 July 2026 extends the EU emissions trading system from 2029 to flights leaving EEA airports for destinations within 5,000 km (North Africa, Turkey, most of the Middle East) and to business jets both ways: about 19-21 Mt of CO₂ a year now outside it. The proposal has still to pass the Parliament and the Council.

rows.label: EU trading extension: share of the newly covered CO₂ actually cut
rows.explainer: Paying for allowances (about €70-90 a tonne) raises fares on the covered routes by a few per cent, so fewer and fuller flights; and the covered emissions must be matched by allowances under a declining cap, cutting elsewhere unless the cap is raised to make room for them. Our judgment, 10% of the covered CO₂: the fare effect alone with air travel's price elasticity of about −0.6 to −1 is a few per cent; up to 40% if the extension adds little to the cap. Rerouting through hubs outside the scope (Istanbul, Dubai) is the counterfactual row below, not here.

rows.label: Share of a won climate policy due to advocacy at all (all groups together)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: climate.advocacy_share_of_policy_win, 30%, 10% to 60%): the part of a won climate policy that is advocates' doing rather than what governments and industry would have done anyway. Both branches take it; each policy's chance of being adopted at all is its own row, and Opportunity Green's part of the advocates' work is each branch's attribution row.

rows.label: IMO Net-Zero Framework: chance it is adopted and enters into force

source.title: Climate Home News (1 May 2026), Key green shipping talks to be held in late 2026
source.note: The adjourned session resumes on 4 December 2026. The October 2025 session voted to adjourn adoption by a year (IUMI newsletter, December 2025, https://iumi.com/newsletter-december-2025/imos-mepcs-extraordinary-session-and-the-delay-of-the-net-zero-framework/). At MEPC 84 a similarly sized group of states pushed to reopen the negotiations (gCaptain, May 2026).

rows.explainer: The framework was approved in April 2025 but its adoption was adjourned in October 2025 under pressure from the United States and oil-producing states; it stays on the table, with the decision due on 4 December 2026. One chance, not a share of many (normalization.md 2.18). Our judgment, 35% (15% to 60%): at MEPC 84 a group about as large as its backers pushed to reopen it, and an adopted text may be weaker (the delivered-share row).

rows.label: EU trading extension to flights within 5,000 km: chance it is adopted

source.title: Beveridge & Diamond (July 2026), European Commission proposes to extend EU ETS to international flights beyond Europe, puts CORSIA on trial
source.note: Published 17 July 2026; it must still pass the Council and the Parliament; ICAO, IATA and Airlines for America oppose it, and non-EU countries may push back.

rows.explainer: A Commission proposal inside the wider trading-system review; the 2012 attempt to cover international flights was suspended under foreign pressure ('stop the clock'). Our judgment, 50% (25% to 75%) that the extension passes roughly as proposed.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Years from the period's spending until the tonnes are avoided
rows.explainer: From the middle of the period's spending (about mid-2025: the charity grew fast) to the policies' own first years: the trading extension from 2029 as proposed; the framework's first compliance year 2028 as approved, a year or more later after the adjournment. Our judgment, 4 years (3 to 6, if adoption or the start slips). Both branches take it.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the tonnes are avoided
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate; the unit's conversion then discounts the heat deaths from the year the tonne is avoided, so nothing is discounted twice.

Expected tonnes averted before adjustments, per period year

rows.explainer: Weights the smoke factor by branch, before waits and years counted, which can't feed a conversion row (docs/normalization.md 2.5).

rows.label: Share of these tonnes from burning less fossil fuel near people
rows.explainer: Both branches cut oil burned: ships' fuel oil replaced by biofuels, LNG and later e-fuels, and jet fuel on flights not flown. Our judgment, all of it (down to 80% for the part of shipping's cut that is methane from LNG, which carries little smoke). How much smoke these fuels carry per tonne is the next row.

rows.label: Deaths a year from ships' air pollution, with 2020's low-sulphur fuel

source.title: Sofiev et al. (2018), Cleaner fuels for ships provide public health benefits with climate tradeoffs, Nature Communications 9: 406
source.quote: low-sulphur marine fuels will still account for ~250k deaths and ~6.4 M childhood asthma cases annually

rows.explainer: Fine particles from ships' exhaust after the 2020 sulphur cap. Range: 150,000 to the 400,000 the same study finds without the cap.

rows.label: CO₂ from all shipping a year (2018)

source.title: IMO (2020), Fourth IMO Greenhouse Gas Study, key findings
source.quote: have increased from 977 million tonnes in 2012 to 1,076 million tonnes in 2018 (9.6% increase)
source.note: Greenhouse gases in CO₂e; CO₂ alone 1,056 million tonnes in 2018 (the same key findings).

rows.explainer: To turn the deaths into deaths per tonne of CO₂ burned at sea.

rows.label: Share of a shipping tonne's smoke deaths avoided when the tonne is cut by switching fuel
rows.explainer: The framework's early cuts come mostly from blending biofuels and from LNG: biofuels carry no sulphur and less soot, LNG almost none of either, but engines still emit nitrogen oxides, which make much of ships' particle pollution, and the fuel is still burned. Our judgment, 30% of the smoke per tonne cut (10% to 60%).

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per shipping tonne cut, relative to the fossil-fuel average
rows.explainer: Ships' deaths per tonne of CO₂ (about 2.4 per 10,000 tonnes, above the fossil-fuel average of 1.46 behind the shared rate) times the share a fuel switch avoids.

rows.label: Deaths a year from civil aviation's air pollution (2006 emissions)

source.title: Yim et al. (2015), Global, regional and local health impacts of civil aviation emissions, Environmental Research Letters 10: 034001
source.quote: finding that aviation emissions cause ∼16 000 (90% CI: 8300–24 000) premature deaths per year

rows.explainer: Deaths from aviation's fine particles and ozone, cruise and airport emissions together. The range is the study's 90% interval.

rows.label: Civil aviation's fuel burn in the same study (2006)

source.title: Yim et al. (2015), Environmental Research Letters 10: 034001, section 2.1
source.quote: Total global fuel burn is estimated to be 188 Tg, of which 36% occurs in North America, 25% in Europe and 20% in Asia.

rows.explainer: 188 million tonnes of jet fuel.

rows.label: CO₂ per kilogram of jet fuel burned

source.title: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2018/2066 on the monitoring and reporting of greenhouse gas emissions, Annex III
source.page: Annex III, table of emission factors for aviation fuels
source.quote: Jet kerosene (Jet A1 or Jet A) 3,15

rows.explainer: The EU trading system's emission factor for jet fuel, tonnes of CO₂ per tonne burned.

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per aviation tonne cut, relative to the fossil-fuel average
rows.explainer: A flight not flown avoids all its smoke: about 0.27 deaths per 10,000 tonnes of CO₂, much of it emitted at cruise height far from people, a fifth of the fossil-fuel average.

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per tonne of these fuels, relative to the fossil-fuel average
rows.explainer: The two branches' smoke factors, weighted by their expected tonnes a year.

rows.label: Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne
rows.explainer: Read by the tco2e unit's conversion (docs/normalization.md 2.5).

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths averted per tonne, counted directly (none here)
rows.explainer: No source counts these policies' deaths directly beside the tonnes; the smoke is in air_pollution_weight, so nothing is counted twice.

rows.label: Share of these tonnes that are methane
rows.explainer: Both cuts are almost all CO₂ from oil. Ships switching to LNG emit some unburned methane, which the framework's well-to-wake accounting counts against them; its part of the net cut is small and uncertain in sign, so it is left at 0 and covered by the evidence rows.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment: how far the modelled tonnes should be trusted
rows.explainer: The tonnes are ex-ante modelling (T&E on the IMO's impact assessment; our own share for the trading extension), not measured cuts. Our judgment, 0.8 (0.5 to 1.1), as in our model of Clean Air Task Force's rule tonnes; adoption and delivery are separate rows. Applied to both branches.

rows.label: IMO branch: share of the counted cut that is real once crop biofuels' land-use emissions are included

source.title: Transport & Environment (April 2025), IMO Net-Zero Framework: assessing the impact of the IMO's draft Net-Zero Framework
source.quote: This could come at a significant cost for the global climate as it is unclear how indirect land-use change (ILUC) emissions will be accounted for under the IMO life cycle analysis guidelines.

rows.explainer: The framework does not cap crop-based biofuels, the cheapest way to meet its early targets; their indirect land-use emissions (forests and grassland cleared to grow the crops elsewhere) can triple a palm biodiesel's footprint and are not yet in the IMO's life-cycle rules. Our judgment, 70% of the counted cut is real (30% if palm and soy oil dominate, 100% if the life-cycle rules shut them out).

rows.label: IMO branch: share of the cut that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Without a global measure, the EU's FuelEU Maritime and trading system (shipping to and from Europe, a minority of the world fleet's fuel) and owners' own plans would make some of these cuts in the first years. Our judgment, 80% (60% to 95%).

rows.label: IMO branch: Opportunity Green's share of the advocates' resources behind the framework

source.title: Opportunity Green, Report and Financial Statements for the Year Ended 31 March 2026 (audited, Sayer Vincent LLP), Charity Commission register
source.quote: 45 countries received our briefings to support them ahead of the IMO negotiations

rows.explainer: Opportunity Green briefs and supports climate-vulnerable delegations (Pacific and other small island states) with legal, technical and policy work at every IMO greenhouse-gas meeting, one of few groups doing so directly. Many others work the file: the Clean Shipping Coalition's members (Transport & Environment, Seas at Risk, Pacific Environment, the Environmental Defense Fund and others), the ICCT and UMAS on research, industry coalitions for ambition, and the funders behind them; climate-vulnerable and European states lead the negotiations themselves (their part is outside advocacy's share). Its shipping work is roughly a third to half of a budget of £2.5 million a year, against a field of tens of millions of dollars a year. Our judgment, 3% (1% to 8%).

rows.label: IMO branch: share of credit used
IMO branch: share of Opportunity Green's work toward adoption done in the period
rows.explainer: Adoption, if it comes, will also rest on the work of 2026 and after, which this period's spending did not pay for; the credit for the period is its share of the charity's whole effort on the framework. Work since 2021 led to the 2023 strategy and the April 2025 approval; more is still needed through the December 2026 decision and its follow-up. Our judgment, 60% (40% to 85%).

rows.label: IMO branch: share of the framework's cut delivered once adopted
rows.explainer: Prices after 2030 are not yet set, ships may pay rather than switch, the adopted text may be weakened (the United States pressed for alternatives without a carbon price), and states that object may not apply it. Our judgment, 60% (30% to 85%), for the tonnes and their compliance costs; the Fund's revenue has its own row.

rows.label: Trading branch: share of the cut that wouldn't have happened anyway, after leakage

source.title: ICCT (July 2026), carbon leakage from a higher EU ETS aviation price (report ID 656)
source.note: Studies the risk that passengers reroute through hubs outside the scope.

rows.explainer: Some passengers will connect through Istanbul or the Gulf to avoid the price, and CORSIA's offsets would have covered part of these flights' growth anyway. Our judgment, 70% (40% to 90%).

rows.label: Trading branch: Opportunity Green's share of the advocates' resources behind the extension

source.title: Opportunity Green, Report and Financial Statements for the Year Ended 31 March 2026 (audited, Sayer Vincent LLP), Charity Commission register
source.quote: It's the only industry body that is supporting the critical expansion of the EU's flagship climate policy: the Emissions Trading System (ETS) to international flights.

rows.explainer: Opportunity Green runs the SASHA Coalition of 18 e-fuel and zero-emission aviation and shipping companies, which backed the extension in Brussels, wrote with Carbon Market Watch to the Commission, and argued for it before the Irish parliament ahead of Ireland's Council presidency. Transport & Environment, Carbon Market Watch, Stay Grounded and others campaign on the same file, and member states and the Commission's own review drive it. Our judgment, 4% (1% to 10%).

rows.label: Trading branch: share of credit used
Trading branch: share of Opportunity Green's work toward adoption done in the period
rows.explainer: The proposal came in July 2026, after the period; the legislative fight in 2026-2028 is still ahead and will take more of the charity's work. Our judgment, 50% (30% to 80%).

rows.label: Trading branch: share of the cut delivered once adopted
rows.explainer: The extension could be scaled back at the 2032 review if CORSIA is strengthened, or narrowed in the negotiations. Our judgment, 80% (50% to 95%) over the years counted.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): no tonne or dollar is measured for Opportunity Green's work; the policies' effects are modelled and its part in them a judgment. Both branches take it.

rows.label: IMO branch: all adjustments combined (tonnes)
rows.formula: evidence_adj * imo_lifecycle_adj * imo_counterfactual_adj * imo_attribution_share * imo_period_share * imo_implementation_adj * missing_data_adj

rows.label: Trading branch: all adjustments combined
rows.formula: evidence_adj * ets_counterfactual_adj * ets_attribution_share * ets_period_share * ets_implementation_adj * missing_data_adj

rows.label: Share of the tonnes that wouldn't have happened anyway (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The branches' own rows apply; this is their average, weighted by each branch's expected tonnes before adjustments, for reading only.

rows.label: Opportunity Green's share of the resources behind the policies (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (imo_downstream * imo_counterfactual_adj * imo_attribution_share_shared + ets_downstream * ets_counterfactual_adj * ets_attribution_share_shared) / (imo_downstream * imo_counterfactual_adj + ets_downstream * ets_counterfactual_adj)
rows.explainer: For reading only; each branch applies its own share.

rows.label: Share of credit used (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches' shares (imo_attribution_share, ets_attribution_share), for reading only; each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Other work of the period not modelled, as a share of the modelled tonnes
rows.explainer: The period's other work has won little that can be counted yet: the challenge to the EU Taxonomy's 'green' label for fossil-fuelled planes and ships (heard in February 2026, judgment pending), the advertising rulings against cruise lines' LNG claims (eight ticket sellers withdrew their ads), the complaint against ArcelorMittal under the OECD guidelines, work on airport caps, aviation fuel tax, data centres and trucking, and the SASHA Coalition's e-fuel proposals. Their spending is in the cost. Our judgment, 10% of the modelled tonnes (0 to 40%), small because none has yet changed a rule.

rows.label: All adjustments combined (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The branches' own combined adjustments apply; this is their average, weighted by each branch's expected tonnes before adjustments, for reading only.

rows.label: IMO branch: share of the compliance cost borne in low- and middle-income countries

source.title: UNCTADstat, Maritime transport insights
source.note: 59% of world seaborne trade by volume reached developing economies in 2024.

rows.explainer: Shipping's higher fuel costs pass through freight rates into the prices of traded goods, so the cost falls on importers and their consumers (and shipowners) roughly by their share of seaborne imports by volume, since fuel cost follows tonne-miles, not value: developing economies received 59% of world seaborne trade in 2024 (UNCTADstat), some of them high-income (Korea, Singapore, the Gulf), and part of the cost falls on exporters and owners. Our judgment, 50% (35% to 60%).

rows.label: IMO branch: consumption per person of those payers in low- and middle-income countries (survey scale, US dollars)
rows.explainer: Household consumption per person on the national accounts is about $2,900-3,000 in Egypt and the Philippines, $5,200 in Peru and $12,500 in Romania (facts: survey_consumption, 2024); China's is higher; surveys find less than the national accounts. Our judgment, $3,000 on the survey scale (1,500 to 6,000); the shared payer multiple (owners and buyers of traded goods are better off than average) applies on top.

rows.label: IMO branch: value lost per dollar of compliance cost, units of value
rows.explainer: Money lost by those who bear the cost, valued on the log scale (docs/normalization.md 2.21): rich-country payers at the shared payer multiple times UK consumption per person on the survey scale (the site's European figure, used for the rich importers), the rest at the shared multiple times the row above. A dollar lost by a poorer payer counts for more.

rows.label: IMO branch: compliance costs, units of value (negative)
rows.formula: -@compliance_costs.imo_nzf_abatement_cost_per_tco2e * @cpi.usa_2025 / @cpi.usa_2023 * imo_tonnes_per_year * imo_payer_uov_per_dollar * imo_p_adopted * p_success * discounted_years * imo_counterfactual_adj * imo_attribution_share * imo_period_share * imo_implementation_adj * missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The framework's compliance cost (docs/normalization.md 2.21): ships' extra fuel cost per tonne cut (facts: compliance_costs.imo_nzf_abatement_cost_per_tco2e, the IMO's own comprehensive impact assessment, $300 in 2023 dollars, moved to 2025's by US consumer prices) times the tonnes the rule counts (before the land-use step, which is about the benefits), valued as money lost by its payers; over the same years and wait as the tonnes, with the branch's chance, counterfactual, credit, period share, delivered share (the tonnes') and missing-data step, not its evidence steps. Remedial-unit payments to the Fund are transfers and left out. The trading extension has no row: no impact analysis we found gives its resource cost (allowance payments are transfers), and its abatement cost, at most the allowance price of about €80 a tonne on a tenth of 20 Mt with this branch's small chance and credit, is under 2% of the shipping compliance term, so it is left out.

rows.label: IMO branch: share of the just-transition money that replaces donors' own climate aid

source.title: UNFCCC decision 1/CMA.6, New collective quantified goal on climate finance (Baku, 2024), para. 8
source.note: Developed countries' goal of $300 billion a year by 2035 counts finance 'from a wide variety of sources, public and private, bilateral and multilateral, including alternative sources'.

rows.explainer: Rich donors may count the Fund's disbursements toward their climate-finance goal, which admits alternative sources such as levies, and give less of their own aid to the same countries. Our judgment, 15% of the money replaces aid that would have come anyway (0 to 40%).

rows.label: IMO branch: share of the Fund's projected income collected once adopted
rows.explainer: Weakening amendments, states that don't apply the framework and lower post-2030 prices cut the revenue, but ships that pay rather than switch fuels raise it, so it falls less than the tonnes. Our judgment, 80% (50% to 100%).

rows.label: IMO branch: just-transition funding for climate-vulnerable countries, units of value
rows.formula: imo_fund_revenue_per_year * imo_jet_share * (@aid_value.development_vs_cash - imo_jet_displaced_share * @aid_value.oda_vs_cash) * @cash.uov_per_dollar * evidence_adj * imo_p_adopted * p_success * discounted_years * imo_attribution_share * imo_period_share * imo_revenue_delivered_adj * missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: Aid won is worth what that aid does (docs/normalization.md 2.20). The Fund's uses are of a known kind: the IMO lists infrastructure, research, technology transfer, training, capacity building and help for small island and least developed states, none of it health or relief, so a dollar of development aid of that kind (facts: aid_value.development_vs_cash, half of cash) times cash to the very poor (facts: cash.uov_per_dollar). Less the donors' own aid it replaces, valued as a dollar of a donor's aid budget (facts: aid_value.oda_vs_cash), since that is what the recipients lose; times the evidence adjustment, since the revenue and its split are the same ex-ante modelling as the tonnes; same years, wait, chance, credit and period share as the tonnes, and its own delivered share. The yearly figure is the first five years' and is held flat over the years a won reform counts (a judgment: T&E's fuel-rewards-first case has none left after 2031). The ships' payments are not netted against it: public money's cost to its payers waits for a site-wide rule (pending), so this gain is gross. The Fund's rewards for clean fuels buy tonnes already in the framework's projected cut and are not counted again.

rows.label: Money effects of the IMO branch, units of value per period year
rows.explainer: The just-transition funding less the compliance costs, per year of the period, in the main chain.

rows.label: The IMO branch's money effects, in tonnes of CO₂e
rows.formula: uov_per_year / (($deaths_per_tco2e * $climate_heat_share * ((1 - methane_share) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -$climate_heat_death_delay + methane_share * @climate.methane_heat_deaths_vs_co2 * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -@climate.methane_heat_death_delay) * (1 + @climate.nondeath_damages_vs_deaths) * (@death_ages.heat_share_under5 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_under5 + @death_ages.heat_share_5_14 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_5_14 + @death_ages.heat_share_15_49 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_15_49 + @death_ages.heat_share_50plus * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_50_74) + ($deaths_per_tco2e * (1 - $climate_heat_share) * air_pollution_weight + extra_deaths_per_tco2e + methane_share * @climate.ozone_deaths_per_tco2e_methane / (1 + ln(1 + $discount_rate) * @climate.methane_lifetime_years)) * (@death_ages.air_pollution_share_under5 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_under5 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_5_14 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_5_14 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_15_49 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_15_49 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_50plus * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_50_74)) * $life_value_multiplier)
rows.explainer: Units of value into tonnes at what a tonne of these is worth on the site's scale (its heat and air-pollution deaths by age, as the conversion counts them), the bridge our other climate models use (docs/normalization.md 2.6).

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e averted per period year, with the money effects in tonnes
rows.formula: (imo_downstream * imo_total_adj + ets_downstream * ets_total_adj) / period_years * (1 + unmodelled_benefits_adj) + tco2e_from_uov
rows.explainer: Each branch's expected tonnes × its own adjustments, summed and spread over the period's four accounting periods, with the other work added as a share; then the IMO branch's just-transition funding less its compliance costs, in tonnes.
